findings.source_passage: shorn of its glamour, it seemed to be turning to grim reality. Tommy--that was all that mattered.
findings.source_locator: third paragraph of source, reflection on the mission turning sinister
findings.why_it_matters: The source's explicit pivot — 'Tommy—that was all that mattered' — is the emotional keystone of this reflection; the draft renders it as vague summary ('the mission looked sinister, its romance shorn off') and drops the signature direct statement entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the phrase 'Tommy—that was all that mattered' as a sentence fragment in the opening paragraph where Tuppence's feelings about the mission's darkening are described.

findings.source_passage: He might be slow, but he was very sure.
findings.source_locator: second paragraph, conclusion of Tuppence's reflection on Tommy vs. Julius
findings.why_it_matters: This is a textually distinctive, rhythmically complete characterisation of Tommy — a signature Christie sentence-shape that defines the Tommy/Julius contrast and anchors Tuppence's emotional dependence. The draft elides it entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Add 'He might be slow, but he was very sure.' at the end of the comparative reflection on Tommy and Julius in the opening section.

findings.source_passage: he tapped with his finger on the table, and Tuppence felt again the intense power that radiated from the man.
findings.source_locator: after Sir James says 'I think it quite likely that I shall be able to make Mrs. Vandemeyer tell me what I want to know'
findings.why_it_matters: This beat establishes Sir James's characterisation as a figure of almost uncanny authority — a motif that recurs throughout the novel and has interpretive weight (he is later revealed as Mr. Brown). Cutting it flattens a deliberate atmospheric signal.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence after Sir James's assurance about Mrs. Vandemeyer: 'He tapped with his finger on the table, and Tuppence felt again the intense power that radiated from the man.'

findings.source_passage: In the moment of victory, Tuppence betrayed a somewhat unsportsmanlike triumph.
findings.source_locator: after Tuppence seizes the revolver and crouches with 'Now who's on top and who's underneath?'
findings.why_it_matters: This narratorial aside is a classic Christie voice-establishing ironic intrusion; its wry, distancing tone is signature Christie and colours the entire revolver-triumph scene. The draft goes straight to the dialogue, erasing the narrator's characteristic wink.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'In the moment of victory, Tuppence betrayed a somewhat unsportsmanlike triumph.' as the sentence immediately preceding her crowing dialogue.

findings.source_passage: I've been afraid.... It's dangerous to know too much! ... Shall I? Shall I ever be?
findings.source_locator: Mrs. Vandemeyer's confession scene, near the end
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves these lines, but the surrounding ellipsis-laden rhythm and Mrs. Vandemeyer's moment of existential dread ('Shall I ever be?') is slightly compressed; the effect is present but attenuated.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor: ensure Mrs. Vandemeyer's fearful lines are set out with the same fragmented punctuation as the source to preserve the sense of barely controlled panic.

summary: Three medium-severity losses — 'Tommy—that was all that mattered,' 'He might be slow, but he was very sure,' and the Sir James power-tap — plus the erasure of the narrator's ironic aside ('somewhat unsportsmanlike triumph') collectively strip voice, characterisation, and an interpretive signal that Christie embeds deliberately; regeneration is required.
